title: Networking L2 / L3
description: Scenario, command, and concept drills for Ethernet, IP routing, and NIC verification

questions.question: A host can ping its default gateway but cannot reach 8.8.8.8. Name the MOST likely layer where the problem sits, and one concrete thing you would check next.
questions.modelAnswer: Layer 3 — check the default route / upstream connectivity beyond the gateway (traceroute, ISP/link).
questions.explanation: Local gateway reachability means L2/L3 to the gateway likely works. Failure beyond that points to routing upstream, ACLs, or WAN issues.

questions.question: What does an ARP request primarily resolve?
options: A hostname to an IPv4 address via recursive DNS
An IPv4 address to a MAC address on the local link
A TCP port to the owning process on Linux
A VLAN ID to a spanning-tree root bridge
questions.explanation: ARP maps IPv4 → MAC so Ethernet can deliver the frame on the local segment.

questions.question: Write a tcpdump command that captures only ICMP traffic on interface eth0 and prints packets verbosely.
questions.explanation: Interface selection (-i), ICMP filter, and verbose (-v) are the key pieces for this capture.

questions.question: Two servers in the same VLAN cannot communicate. ethtool shows both links are UP. Switches show the correct MAC on each port. What protocol mapping would you verify next on the hosts, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: Check ARP/neighbor tables — verify each host has the correct IP→MAC mapping (stale/wrong ARP can break L3 on a healthy L2 path).
questions.explanation: Healthy link + correct switch MAC learning suggests L2 is fine. Wrong or missing ARP entries are a classic next failure mode.

questions.question: How does a router differ from a Layer-2 switch when forwarding?
options: Routers forward between IP subnets using routing tables; switches forward frames in a broadcast domain using MAC tables
Switches decrement IP TTL on every hop while routers never touch TTL
Routers only forward based on destination MAC addresses inside one VLAN
There is no difference once both devices enable jumbo frames
questions.explanation: Switches bridge within an L2 domain; routers interconnect IP networks and make longest-prefix decisions.

questions.scenario: Lab: Host A 10.0.1.10/24 gateway 10.0.1.1. Host B 10.0.2.20/24 gateway 10.0.2.1. Router connects both subnets. A ping from A to B fails. tcpdump on A shows ARP who-has 10.0.2.20 — not an ARP for the gateway.
questions.question: What is wrong with Host A’s networking configuration (one sentence)?
questions.modelAnswer: Host A is missing (or ignoring) a default route to 10.0.1.1, so it ARPs for a remote IP as if it were local.
questions.explanation: ARPing for a remote subnet IP means the host thinks the destination is on-link — classic missing/incorrect default route or mask.

questions.question: Using the ip command, show how you would add a default route via gateway 192.168.1.1 on Linux.
acceptedAnswers: sudo ip route add default via 192.168.1.1
questions.explanation: The modern iproute2 syntax installs a default route through the given next hop.

questions.question: Why is RSS / flow hashing important when verifying multi-queue NICs?
options: It steers packets across receive queues/CPUs; bad hashing causes imbalance or surprising reordering
It replaces BGP as the control plane in leaf-spine fabrics
It compresses Ethernet payloads before DMA into host memory
It forces every protocol onto a single CPU core for determinism
questions.explanation: RSS distributes flows for parallelism. Verification must check balance, affinity, and correctness under multi-queue load.

questions.question: In one sentence, explain what RDMA gives you that classic kernel TCP sockets usually do not.
questions.modelAnswer: RDMA enables low-latency remote memory access with far less CPU involvement than traditional kernel networking paths.
questions.explanation: RDMA/RoCE is about bypassing much of the traditional stack for HPC/AI fabrics — latency and CPU efficiency are the punchline.

questions.scenario: Performance lab: enabling TSO doubles throughput to a peer, but a middlebox that rewrites packets starts dropping sessions only when TSO is on.
questions.question: What class of NIC feature is implicated, and what is your first A/B experiment?
questions.modelAnswer: Segmentation/checksum offloads — A/B by disabling TSO/GSO (and related offloads) with ethtool and retesting through the middlebox.
questions.explanation: Offloads change packet shape on the wire. Interop bugs often appear only when hardware segmentation is enabled.

questions.question: What does a /24 IPv4 prefix length mean?
options: The first 24 bits are the network; typically 256 addresses in the block
Exactly 24 hosts may exist on the subnet with no exceptions
Packets may traverse at most 24 routers before being discarded
The interface MTU must be set to 24 KB for that route

questions.question: Write a Python function `same_subnet(ip1, ip2, prefix)` that returns True if two dotted IPv4 strings are in the same subnet for the given prefix length (0–32). You may use the stdlib.
questions.starterCode:
import ipaddress

def same_subnet(ip1, ip2, prefix):
acceptedAnswers:
n = ipaddress.IPv4Network(f"{ip1}/{prefix}", strict=False)
return ipaddress.IPv4Address(ip2) in n
questions.explanation: Using ipaddress avoids hand-rolled masking bugs and is interview-friendly for networking tooling.

followUpQuestions.question: Which OSI layer owns MAC addresses?
followUpQuestions.explanation: MAC addresses are Layer 2 (Data Link) identifiers.

followUpQuestions.question: Which protocol resolves IPv4 addresses to MAC addresses?
options: DHCP
DNS
ARP
NTP
followUpQuestions.explanation: ARP performs IPv4→MAC resolution on the local link.

followUpQuestions.question: Write a command to display the kernel routing table using iproute2.
followUpQuestions.explanation: ip route (show) prints the routing table.

followUpQuestions.question: Name one reason TTL exists in IP packets.
followUpQuestions.modelAnswer: To prevent packets from looping forever in the network.
followUpQuestions.explanation: TTL/hop limit bounds the lifetime of a packet in the presence of routing loops.

followUpQuestions.question: RoCE is most closely associated with which capability?
followUpQuestions.explanation: RoCE carries RDMA over Converged Ethernet.

Networking L2 / L3 — Study Guide

For the full interactive course, open this section’s Learn path (Basics → Advanced → Expert). Every important command is explained flag-by-flag there.

Level map

  • Basics: How a packet really moves — and the first commands that prove it
  • Advanced: Routes, VLANs, TCP vs UDP, and capture filters that tell a story
  • Expert: NIC offloads, RSS, RDMA — verify like a networking SDK engineer

Free resources

  • Cloudflare Learning Center — Networking — Friendly deep explainers for IP, DNS, TLS, and packets.
  • Practical Networking — Excellent free subnetting and packet-flow lessons.
  • tcpdump man page — Authoritative filter syntax and flags.

tutorial.intro: Learn networking by walking packets through the stack, then mastering the exact Linux commands you will use in labs and interviews — with every flag explained.

levels.title: Basics
levels.tagline: How a packet really moves — and the first commands that prove it
levels.html:
Goal of this level: understand what happens between “press Enter on ping” and “reply comes back”, and use Linux tools to observe each step.

1. The three jobs in networking

  1. Ethernet (Layer 2) delivers frames on one local link/VLAN using MAC addresses.
  2. IP (Layer 3) delivers packets between networks using IP addresses + routes.
  3. TCP/UDP (Layer 4) delivers data to the right app using ports.
Why this split matters

When something fails, you diagnose one layer at a time. “Internet is down” is not a diagnosis — “no default route” or “ARP incomplete” is.

2. See your host’s identity

ip addr show
ip
The modern Linux networking command (iproute2). Prefer this over old ifconfig.
addr
Address subcommand: show/add/delete IP addresses on interfaces.
show
Print current addresses (can omit; ip addr alone also lists them).

In the output, look for:

  • eth0 / ens* / enp* — your NIC name
  • inet 10.0.1.10/24 — IPv4 address and prefix length
  • inet6 ... — IPv6 if present
  • state UP — link is administratively/carrier up
/24 means

The first 24 bits are the network. Hosts with the same first three octets (e.g. 10.0.1.x) are usually on-link. Everything else needs a router (gateway).

3. See how the host forwards packets

ip route show
ip route
Routing table: “for this destination, use this next hop / device.”
show
List routes (default if you type only ip route).

Important lines:

  • default via 10.0.1.1 dev eth0 — if no better match, send to gateway 10.0.1.1 out eth0
  • 10.0.1.0/24 dev eth0 ... — destinations in this subnet are on-link on eth0 (no gateway)

4. ARP: map IP → MAC on the local link

Ethernet cannot send to an “IP”. It sends to a MAC. ARP answers: “Who has 10.0.1.1? Tell 10.0.1.10.”

ip neigh show
ip neigh
Neighbor table (ARP for IPv4, Neighbor Discovery for IPv6).
show
List known IP→MAC (or unresolved) entries.

States you will see: REACHABLE (good), STALE (old but usable), INCOMPLETE/FAILED (ARP did not resolve — big red flag).

5. Ping as a layer test (not a full app test)

ping -c 4 10.0.1.1
ping
Sends ICMP Echo Requests; waits for Echo Replies.
-c 4
Stop after 4 probes (otherwise ping runs forever).
10.0.1.1
Target IP — often your default gateway in labs.
Interpret ping results
  • Gateway ping works, 8.8.8.8 fails → local LAN OK; problem is upstream routing/WAN/DNS separately.
  • Same-subnet ping fails → L2/ARP/VLAN/host firewall before “the internet”.
  • Ping success does not prove TCP port 443 works.

6. First packet capture

sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n icmp
sudo
Packet capture usually needs root or CAP_NET_RAW.
tcpdump
Capture and print packets matching a filter.
-i eth0
Listen on interface eth0 (change to your NIC name).
-n
Do not resolve names — show raw IPs/ports (faster, clearer).
icmp
Capture filter: only ICMP (what ping uses).
Do this once
  1. Terminal A: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n icmp
  2. Terminal B: ping -c 3 10.0.1.1
  3. Confirm you see echo request/reply lines. That is “proof”, not vibes.

levels.title: Advanced
levels.tagline: Routes, VLANs, TCP vs UDP, and capture filters that tell a story
levels.html:
Goal: debug real failures with evidence — wrong route, remote ARP mistake, MTU issues, TCP resets.

1. Add / fix a default route

sudo ip route add default via 192.168.1.1
sudo ip route add
Install a new route in the kernel routing table.
default
Matches every destination that has no more-specific route (same as 0.0.0.0/0).
via 192.168.1.1
Next-hop gateway IP (must be reachable on-link).
sudo ip route del default
del
Remove a route — useful when a bad default was added.
default
Deletes the default route (be careful on remote SSH).
Classic bug you must recognize

Host ARPs for a remote IP (e.g. 10.0.2.20) instead of the gateway. That means it thinks the destination is local — usually missing default route or wrong netmask.

2. Richer captures for debugging

sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nv host 10.0.1.10 and port 443
-v
Verbose: show more protocol detail (TTL, length, etc.).
-n
No DNS/port-name resolution.
host 10.0.1.10
Only packets to/from this IP.
and port 443
And only TCP/UDP port 443 (HTTPS).
and
Combines filter expressions (tcpdump uses pcap filter syntax).
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n arp
arp
Filter: only ARP packets — perfect when you suspect IP→MAC problems.

3. TCP vs UDP (what to say in interviews)

  • TCP: connection setup (handshake), reliable delivery, ordering, congestion control. Use for most APIs.
  • UDP: no connection, no built-in reliability. Use when the app invents its own reliability or latency beats guarantees (or tunnels).
ss -lntp
ss
Socket statistics (modern replacement for much of netstat).
-l
Listening sockets only.
-n
Numeric ports (do not translate 22→ssh).
-t
TCP only.
-p
Show owning process (may need root for others’ processes).
Why ss matters in SDK labs

Before blaming the SDK, confirm something is actually listening on the expected port, and which PID owns it.

4. MTU and “it works for small pings only”

Standard Ethernet MTU is often 1500 bytes for the IP packet. If a path has a smaller MTU and ICMP “Fragmentation Needed” is blocked, large TCP sessions die mysteriously while ping -s small works.

ping -c 3 -M do -s 1472 8.8.8.8
-M do
Path MTU discovery probe: do not fragment.
-s 1472
Payload size. 1472 + 28 byte IP/ICMP headers ≈ 1500 MTU.
8.8.8.8
Replace with a peer on the path you are testing.

5. Troubleshooting order (memorize)

  1. Link: carrier/errors (ip link, ethtool)
  2. L2: VLAN, MAC learning, ARP state
  3. L3: address, mask, routes, ping gateway then beyond
  4. Policy: firewall/iptables/nft/security groups
  5. App: listen port, TLS, timeouts (ss, app logs)

levels.title: Expert
levels.tagline: NIC offloads, RSS, RDMA — verify like a networking SDK engineer
levels.html:
Goal: understand performance-path features that break correctness when misunderstood.

1. ethtool: the NIC control panel

ethtool eth0
ethtool
Query/change NIC driver settings (link mode, speed, offloads, rings).
eth0
Target network interface.

Shows link speed/duplex and whether the link is detected.

ethtool -k eth0
-k
Show offload features: which work the NIC/stack accelerates (checksum, TSO, GRO, etc.).
on/off columns
fixed = cannot change; on/off = current state.
sudo ethtool -K eth0 tso off gso off gro off
-K
Change offload features (capital K).
tso off
Disable TCP Segmentation Offload — CPU segments large TCP sends instead of NIC.
gso off
Disable Generic Segmentation Offload in software.
gro off
Disable Generic Receive Offload aggregation on receive.
Why A/B offloads

Many “perf wins” and many weird middlebox bugs appear only with offloads enabled. Professionals always test both.

ethtool -S eth0
-S
Driver statistics: drops, errors, queue counters — gold for “is the NIC unhappy?”

2. RSS / multi-queue

RSS (Receive Side Scaling) hashes flows to multiple receive queues/CPUs so one core is not the bottleneck.

ethtool -l eth0
-l
Show channel/queue counts (RX/TX/combined).
grep eth0 /proc/interrupts
/proc/interrupts
Kernel table of interrupt counts per CPU.
grep eth0
Filter lines for your NIC IRQs — look for imbalance (all hits on CPU0).
Experienced answer

“I’d check RSS queue count, IRQ affinity, and per-CPU interrupt rates before publishing Gbps numbers — otherwise I’m benchmarking the scheduler, not the NIC.”

3. RDMA / RoCE (high level you must own)

  • RDMA lets one host read/write remote memory with low latency and less CPU than kernel TCP sockets.
  • RoCE is RDMA over Converged Ethernet — common in AI/HPC clusters.
  • Verification concerns: lossy vs lossless fabric, PFC/ECN, connection recovery, interoperability.

4. Expert verification matrix

  • Kernel × driver × firmware
  • Offloads on vs off
  • MTU 1500 vs jumbo
  • Single queue vs multi-queue
  • Peer OS differences
Capstone

Take a working two-host path and break it five ways (bad route, wrong ARP static, VLAN mismatch, MTU black hole, offload+middlebox). For each, write the first three commands and the evidence you expect.
